historical_timeline.summary: Born Cassius Clay in Louisville, Kentucky.
Diagnosed at 42 with a parkinsonian condition by a neurologist in New York.
His physician described the condition in a television interview and said his cognitive function had not declined.
Lit the Olympic cauldron in Atlanta; his hand shook as he held the torch.
Co-founded the Muhammad Ali Parkinson Center in Phoenix.
Died in the Phoenix area at 74.

claims.statement: Muhammad Ali was born Cassius Clay in Louisville, Kentucky, on January 17, 1942.
Ali died on June 3, 2016, in the Phoenix area, at age 74. A family spokesman gave the cause as septic shock due to unspecified natural causes.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Record the death as a fact without detail.

claims.statement: In 1984, at age 42 and three years after he retired from boxing, Ali was diagnosed with a parkinsonian condition by the neurologist Stanley Fahn in New York; it has been publicly described as Parkinson's disease since.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the synthetic Parkinson's disease. Sources label it parkinsonism, Parkinson's syndrome, or Parkinson's disease.

claims.statement: The diagnosing neurologist later said publicly that slowness of movement was Ali's main limitation at the time of diagnosis, with a masked face, decreased blinking, a typical parkinsonian tremor, and a shuffling gait, and that some features were too early for classic Parkinson's disease.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Physician's public account, given after Ali's death.

claims.statement: In a 1996 television interview, Ali's physician Dennis Cope described his condition as Parkinson's syndrome attributed to pugilistic brain syndrome from boxing, and said testing showed his cognitive function had not declined: "His mind is fine."
claims.clinical_interpretation: Physician's public statement; it supports the synthetic normal cognitive screen.

claims.statement: Whether boxing caused Ali's Parkinson's disease is disputed. The diagnosing neurologist thought the early symptoms were probably caused by repeated blows to the head but could not be certain; his later physician Abraham Lieberman did not think boxing contributed, though he was not a hundred percent certain; and the director of the Muhammad Ali Parkinson Center said there was no medical evidence that boxing contributed.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective causal interpretation; not coded as a diagnosis.

claims.statement: As the disease progressed, Ali developed a tremor and his speech became increasingly difficult. When he lit the Olympic cauldron in Atlanta on July 19, 1996, his hand shook as he held the torch.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the tremor and the synthetic soft speech; the cauldron lighting fixes the index year.

claims.statement: Ali, his physician Abraham Lieberman, and a Phoenix philanthropist founded the Muhammad Ali Parkinson Center at the Barrow Neurological Institute in 1997. Lieberman, who was among those who diagnosed him in 1984 and later treated him, said Ali stood up to the disease for 34 years and that in his final years he lost the ability to speak and use his hands.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Physician's public statements after Ali's death; the late-stage details postdate the episode and are not used in it.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Long-term care of a man with young-onset Parkinson's disease twelve years after diagnosis: a structured motor examination and Hoehn and Yahr stage at every visit; levodopa dose and timing adjusted for bradykinesia with supine and standing blood pressure checks; screening for falls, swallowing problems, mood, cognition, sleep, autonomic symptoms, psychosis, and impulse control; speech therapy for soft speech and physical therapy for gait and balance; avoidance of dopamine-blocking drugs; and advance care planning, on the CMID Parkinson's disease schedule with AAN and MDS guidance. The publicly discussed link to boxing is treated as a disputed retrospective interpretation, not a diagnosis.

documentation.chief_complaint: Four-week Parkinson's disease follow-up, seen the same day by movement disorders neurology

hpi.narrative: Mr. Ali is a 54-year-old man with young-onset Parkinson's disease, diagnosed twelve years ago, who returns four weeks after his first visit and is seen by movement disorders neurology on the same day. Slowness of movement is still his main limitation: buttoning, handwriting, and getting out of low chairs take him longer, and he feels the slowness most in the late morning and late afternoon. The right-hand tremor is mild and settles when he uses the hand. People still have trouble hearing him in a crowd. He takes carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 mg one tablet three times a day, often with meals, and has noticed no wearing-off before doses, no involuntary movements, and no lightheadedness on standing. He has had no falls or near falls. He sleeps well, has no dream enactment, and has no hallucinations or new urges to gamble, shop, or eat.

documentation.chief_complaint: Three-month Parkinson's disease review after the levodopa increase and speech therapy

hpi.narrative: Mr. Ali returns three months after his first visit. Since carbidopa-levodopa was increased to one and a half tablets three times a day, taken 30 minutes before meals, he is quicker with buttons and getting out of chairs, and the late-morning slowness has eased. He has had no involuntary movements, no wearing-off before doses, and no lightheadedness on standing, nausea, or sleepiness. He finished the four-week LSVT LOUD speech therapy course two months ago and practices his voice exercises each day; people hear him more easily. He has had six physical therapy sessions and now walks, rides a stationary bicycle, and does balance exercises about 150 minutes a week. He has had no falls. He has had no hallucinations.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Ali is a 54-year-old man with young-onset Parkinson's disease, diagnosed twelve years ago, who comes for his periodic preventive visit four weeks after his six-month Parkinson's disease review. referral.question: Young-onset Parkinson's disease, diagnosed twelve years ago at 42, in a 54-year-old man whose slowness of movement now limits daily tasks on a modest levodopa dose. Please review the diagnosis, advise on the levodopa dose or another agent, and plan rehabilitation for his soft speech and gait
referral.urgency: Routine, within four weeks, on the same day as his four-week primary care check
referral.pertinent_history: Parkinsonism diagnosed at 42, three years after he retired from professional boxing; at the time it was described as a parkinsonian syndrome possibly related to repeated head blows, and that link has never been settled. On carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 mg one tablet three times daily, often taken with meals, for many years. Today, in the on state: MDS-UPDRS Part III 30, Hoehn and Yahr stage 2.5, with bilateral bradykinesia and rigidity worse on the right, right-hand rest tremor, reduced facial expression and blinking, and soft, monotone speech. No dyskinesia, wearing-off, or freezing. No falls; Timed Up and Go 13 seconds; recovers after three steps on the pull test. Blood pressure 130/80 mmHg supine and 122/78 mmHg standing at 3 minutes. MoCA 27 of 30, PHQ-9 3, EAT-10 2, negative REM sleep behavior disorder and impulse-control screens, and Epworth score 6. Blood count, chemistry, vitamin B12, and TSH normal. No dopamine-blocking drugs
questions: Does he meet the MDS criteria for Parkinson's disease, given the young onset and the earlier description of a parkinsonian syndrome related to boxing, and is brain imaging needed?
Should levodopa be increased, or another agent added, for the bradykinesia?
What rehabilitation do you advise for his soft speech and his gait and balance?
How often should he be followed, and by whom?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Ali, a 54-year-old man with parkinsonism diagnosed twelve years ago at 42, is seen at the request of Dr. Moreau. Slowness of movement is his main limitation: buttoning, handwriting, and rising from low chairs take longer, most of all in the late morning and late afternoon. He has a mild right-hand tremor at rest. His voice is soft, and people have trouble hearing him in crowds. He takes carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 mg one tablet three times a day, often with meals, and notices no wearing-off before doses, no involuntary movements, no freezing, and no lightheadedness on standing. He has had no falls, hallucinations, dream enactment, or new urges to gamble, shop, or eat. He boxed professionally until three years before the diagnosis
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Moreau's first-visit assessment four weeks ago: MDS-UPDRS Part III 30, Hoehn and Yahr stage 2.5, Timed Up and Go 13 seconds, pull test, supine and standing blood pressure, MoCA 27, PHQ-9 3, EAT-10 2, sleep and impulse-control screens; blood count, chemistry, vitamin B12, and TSH from the same visit; and today's supine and standing blood pressure

assessment.assessment: Clinically established Parkinson's disease by the MDS criteria: bradykinesia with rest tremor and rigidity, a clear and lasting response to levodopa, and no red flags or absolute exclusions. There is no early falling, no vertical gaze palsy, no cerebellar or pyramidal sign, no early autonomic failure, and no early dementia. Whether repeated blows to the head in his boxing career contributed cannot be confirmed or excluded during life. The course and examination are those of Parkinson's disease, and the question does not change his treatment

assessment.display: Bradykinesia on a modest levodopa dose
assessment.assessment: Bradykinesia limits daily tasks on levodopa 100 mg three times daily, with no motor complications. Taking doses with meals blunts absorption. Raising levodopa is the simplest and best-tolerated step. A dopamine agonist would add risks of sleepiness, impulse-control disorders, and hallucinations, and an MAO-B inhibitor would add only a small benefit
Soft, monotone speech typical of Parkinson's disease, which responds well to intensive voice treatment
No falls, but short steps and a three-step pull-test recovery show early postural instability. Supervised exercise and balance training lower fall risk and improve gait
Genetic testing with counseling is now offered to everyone with Parkinson's disease, and young onset makes it more informative. The result would not change his current treatment

recommendations: Increase carbidopa-levodopa to one and a half 25/100 mg tablets (levodopa 150 mg) three times daily, taken 30 minutes before meals, and spread protein through the day
Check supine and three-minute standing blood pressure at the next visit after the increase; report lightheadedness, involuntary movements, nausea, or sleepiness
No dopamine agonist or MAO-B inhibitor for now; review if motor fluctuations appear
Avoid dopamine-blocking drugs (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, and antipsychotics other than quetiapine, clozapine, or pimavanserin); use ondansetron if an antiemetic is needed
Four-week intensive speech therapy course (LSVT LOUD), then daily voice practice
Physical therapy for gait and balance, building to at least 150 minutes a week of aerobic, strength, and balance exercise
No brain imaging or laboratory workup is needed, because there are no atypical features
Genetic testing with counseling offered today; he will decide at the yearly review

Primary care follows him every three months on the CMID schedule, with motor examination, Hoehn and Yahr stage, fall check, orthostatic blood pressure, and psychosis and impulse-control questions at each visit, and cognition, mood, sleep, autonomic, swallowing, and speech screens yearly
